overview: This card’s “Tibetans” label belongs to the atlas, not to a known Bronze Age nation. From about 1500 to 500 BCE, the map paints one enormous shape across the Tibetan Plateau and far beyond. Archaeology instead reveals many local communities in valleys, grasslands, basins and Himalayan corridors. At sites such as Qugong, Changguogou, Bangga and Gepaseru, people combined crops, herds, hunting, craft and exchange in different ways. Barley and wheat tolerated cold highlands; sheep, goats, cattle, horses and eventually securely identified domestic yak helped turn grass into food, fiber, transport and fuel. Tiny clues do surprising work: charred seeds reveal meals, animal teeth track movement, and hardened dental plaque preserves milk proteins, an ancient snack record no toothbrush could erase. The evidence does not name everyone’s language, government or beliefs. Tibetan writing, the Tibetan Empire and state-supported Buddhism appear more than a thousand years after this card ends, so they must not be pasted backward. At 500 BCE the atlas polygon simply disappears. People, farms, herds, routes and regional cultures continued; only this broad editorial category stopped.

periods.title: A map umbrella meets dated communities
periods.summary: The first atlas layer draws one border from roughly 76.5°E to 105.3°E and 27.1°N to 43.0°N. Dated evidence instead comes from particular places: mixed crops at Changguogou and Qugong, early dairy at Gepaseru, and Himalayan ancestry samples. These discoveries illuminate networks and adaptations, not one polity or frontier.

periods.title: Local traditions change inside an unchanged polygon
periods.summary: The atlas reuses exactly the same geometry at 1000 BCE, while excavation shows change. Central Tibetan ceramics, stone tools, crop processing and settlement organization did not stay frozen. Regional exchange continued, and evidence for metal, livestock and mobility varies sharply by site and date.

periods.title: First-millennium diversity, then an editorial seam
periods.summary: A slightly redrawn atlas polygon covers the final interval. Bangga and other first-millennium sites document agropastoral choices, corrals, grinding and changing pottery; later parts of that evidence must be kept within their dates. At 500 BCE the exact id vanishes. No conquest or population disappearance is established by that map change.

sections.title: Read the map before imagining a country

items.text: The live index calls this exact record “Tibetans,” classifies it as a culture and assigns approximate dates of 1500 to 500 BCE. Those fields identify an atlas feature. They do not establish an ancient self-name, census, capital, government, common language or surveyed border.

The old imported summary describes present-day population totals and modern administrative regions. That information is centuries out of place for a Bronze and early Iron Age card. The replacement begins with dated archaeology and clearly separates modern Tibetan identities from unnamed prehistoric communities.

At 1500 and 1000 BCE the target geometry is byte-for-byte identical: one simple polygon stretching from near Hotan and Leh to Chengdu and Xining. A thousand kilometres of mountains, basins and valleys cannot be treated as a single excavated cultural zone because a digital outline encloses them.

At 700 BCE one coordinate changes and the geometry hash changes, yet every tested target point remains inside. At 500 BCE the id is absent everywhere tested. These are cartographic seams; neither a one-point edit nor feature deletion proves migration, conquest, ethnic replacement or collapse.

The atlas previously labels parts of the region “Tibeto-Burmanese” and later applies “Proto-Tibetan cultures,” but archaeology cannot certify a tidy relay between those categories. Pots, genes and crops can show contact or descent patterns; none records the map-maker’s sequence as an ancient family tree.

Archaeologists excavate layer by layer, record where objects lie and date short-lived material such as charred grain. At Bangga, flotation recovered tiny plant remains, while pottery, stone tools, animal bones and architecture were studied together. A loose bronze object without context answers far fewer questions.

Direct radiocarbon dates on barley and wheat matter because an undated seed might have slipped into an older layer. Large site syntheses then compare altitude, crop species and domestic animals. Their famous “after 3600 BP” pattern is a regional trend, not one exact settlement date for the entire plateau.

Surface stone artifacts are especially hard to date because wind, water, trampling and burial move them. Optically stimulated luminescence can estimate when a stone surface was buried, but researchers also study sediment and landforms. The clever machine does not cancel the need for careful context.

At Nwya Devu, Chusang and Baishiya, stone tools, footprints, sediment, fossils, proteins and DNA show much older high-altitude visits or occupation. They are essential background, but their makers lived thousands to more than one hundred thousand years before this card; they cannot be renamed “Tibetans” here.

Ancient DNA can compare sampled individuals, estimate close kinship and reveal ancestry change. It cannot hear a dead person speak or read their political loyalties. Plateau genome studies show continuity and repeated interaction, so this card reports population history without turning a genetic cluster into a nation.

sections.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments

items.text: The plateau is not one endless snowy table. Cold desert, dry steppe, alpine meadow, warmer river valleys, basins and forested eastern margins offer different water, fuel, crops and pasture. Later ecological surveys help describe that variety, but they are environmental comparison rather than a Bronze Age land-use census.

At roughly 4,000 metres, each breath contains much less oxygen than at sea level. Present-day Tibetan populations carry strongly selected high-altitude variants, including a Denisovan-related EPAS1 haplotype. That deep inheritance illuminates biology, yet it cannot identify which excavated potter carried it without ancient DNA.

Cold, aridity and surprise snow made resilience a household problem. Communities could spread risk across crops, grazing, stored food, dairy and exchange instead of trusting one harvest. Pollen, charcoal and other environmental proxies show mountain landscapes changing through long interaction between climate, vegetation and people.

Warm valleys could support fields while broad uplands offered seasonal pasture. Mobility models suggest repeated farmer to herder interaction corridors, but their pathways are calculated possibilities checked against artifacts, not GPS tracks from 800 BCE. Real routes shifted with grass, snow, water, kin and exchange partners.

The giant atlas polygon includes places with sharply different rainfall and growing seasons, even though its outline barely changes for centuries. Archaeological evidence therefore works best as a mosaic: a claim about Qugong or Qaidam stays local unless several independently dated sites justify a broader pattern.

At Changguogou, researchers identified naked barley, wheat and foxtail millet. Their coexistence matters: western-origin wheat and barley met an eastern millet tradition in central Tibet. People were choosing a mixed menu and crop-risk strategy, not instantly replacing every older plant with one “Tibetan” staple.

Barley and wheat tolerate colder growing conditions than millet and helped farming reach higher elevations. Regional evidence after about 1600 BCE combines these grains with sheep and other livestock. Elevation still mattered: some communities farmed valleys, while people in non-arable highlands depended more heavily on animals.

Dental calculus, the hard plaque a dentist scrapes away, preserved milk proteins in ancient mouths. At Gepaseru, goat-milk protein dates to about 1500 to 1312 BCE. That is a wonderfully unglamorous archive: somebody’s stubborn tooth crust became a tiny, scientifically readable receipt for dairy consumption.

Grinding stones at Qugong, Changguogou and Bangga could turn barley or wheat into flour. Bangga vessel forms and tool assemblages suggest flour-based cooking, but no surviving recipe says “make this exact bread.” Porridge, dough or roasted flour remain possibilities only where residues or cooking traces support them.

Plant and animal finds also leave room for hunting, fishing and gathering alongside farming and herding. Their proportions changed by region. A family in a productive valley, a mobile highland camp and a basin settlement did not necessarily eat alike, even if the atlas colors them identically.

Sheep and goats converted short highland grasses into meat, milk, hides and fiber. Their bones occur widely, while animal genomes help trace long dispersals. A sheep lineage is still not a human ethnicity: animals can be traded, stolen, exchanged at marriage or moved between communities speaking different languages.

Qugong animal remains suggested possible yak and sheep in the second millennium BCE, but secure domestic-yak evidence is later. At Bangga around 2500 BP, ancient DNA identifies domestic yak, taurine cattle and hybrids. The card preserves that sequence instead of granting every earlier large bovine a yak passport.

Bangga herders kept sheep, goats, cattle, yak or hybrids and horses. Different animals supplied different combinations of meat, milk, fiber, traction and transport, buffering bad weather or disease. Manure in a corral also became fertilizer or fuel, the least glamorous part of the herd could still keep a hearth useful.

Qaidam surveys found smaller, sometimes ephemeral high-altitude structures with barley, wheat, grinding tools and bones of horses, cattle, sheep and dogs. This supports flexible agro-pastoral mobility in that basin. It does not prove that every household moved seasonally or followed the same annual circuit.

Upper Mustang’s Kali Gandaki corridor links plateau and South Asian lowlands, while modeling identifies other likely corridors across grasslands and valleys. Goods, animals, stories and marriage partners could travel in stages. Calling these links a prehistoric “Silk Road” would be catchy but chronologically misleading.

Bangga preserves stone foundations, rooms, enclosures and a corral-like area rather than a palace or city grid. Architecture suggests repeated agropastoral occupation, but building use can change. Archaeologists compare floors, hearths, dung, artifacts and repairs before deciding whether a space sheltered people, animals or supplies.

Qugong’s second-millennium ceramics include finely polished black wares and distinctive ring-footed forms; first-millennium Bangga pottery differs while retaining a few local practices. Pots therefore reveal skilled choices and contact, not an ethnic barcode. The same household could imitate, trade or reject a neighboring style.

Spindle whorls and rare fabric traces from the southeastern plateau show people spinning fiber and weaving. Some later Bronze Age graves contain more costly textile tools, hinting at status differences. Because cloth decays easily and graves are selective, archaeologists cannot reconstruct one standard outfit for all communities.

Cold-weather clothing probably required layered plant fiber, wool, hair, hide or fur, but exact combinations must remain site-specific. Animal management made fiber and skins available; textile tools show production. A modern yak-hair tent or robe may inspire questions, yet it cannot serve as a photograph of 1000 BCE.

Copper, bronze, iron and mixed-metal objects enter different plateau regions on uneven schedules. Composite objects and imported forms show experimentation and exchange. Metal did not erase stone or bone tools overnight, and a bronze style cannot by itself identify a migrant, ruler or language community.

No household list names parents, grandparents or adopted children in this interval. Houses, shared work areas, graves and ancient DNA can test possible relationships, but each captures only part of social life. The safest picture is cooperating households and networks whose exact kin rules remain unknown.

Milk proteins occur in women and men, adults and children, and both richer and plainer burials. That result gives people of different ages and statuses a rare presence in food history. It does not tell who milked, churned or controlled herds, so those jobs should not be assigned automatically by gender.

Spinning tools show substantial textile labor, and differences among graves may reflect organized production or status. Some workers were likely highly practiced, but the objects do not announce “women’s work” or “men’s work.” Sexed skeletons, use-wear and workshop context are needed before making that claim.

Children had to learn animal behavior, safe routes, crop timing, tool handling, food preparation and local social rules. There is no evidence for a Bronze Age school or Tibetan alphabet lesson. Skill probably grew through watching, helping and practice, an inference from household production rather than a surviving timetable.

Burials include people of different ages, and cave or cist traditions vary across the plateau and Himalayas. A child buried with objects is not a simple measure of affection, rank or inheritance. Mortuary choices concern survivors and ritual as well as the dead, so comparisons require dates and local context.

sections.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question

items.text: Thin air, cold, smoke, injuries, childbirth, infection and food shortage all posed risks, yet this card has no contemporary medical manual. Healed bone can show survival after injury and teeth can preserve disease or diet. It cannot name the herb, helper or ritual used during recovery.

High-Himalayan skeletons show that dental disease and childhood stress differed between sites rather than following one altitude rule. Those studied communities span other dates and places, so they offer method and comparison. They cannot be pasted wholesale onto Qugong or every person inside the atlas polygon.

Dental calculus can preserve food proteins as well as the microbial mineral layer itself. Researchers sampled it carefully, checked preservation and identified peptides. Finding milk protein proves consumption far more securely than guessing from a pot shape; failing to find it, however, does not prove someone never drank milk.

Settlements depended on springs, streams, rivers, snowmelt and seasonal water, but published evidence does not establish one managed water system for this umbrella. Households had to separate drinking, cooking, animals and refuse somehow. The exact containers, rules and daily fetching duties vary or remain archaeologically invisible.

No securely identified toilet, latrine or sewer is attributable to this exact atlas category and interval. Corrals and manure deposits show that people managed at least some animal waste, but human sanitation leaves weaker traces. It would be irresponsible to invent either palace plumbing or a universal “go outside” rule.

sections.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits

items.text: Stone-cist, cave and other graves, animal offerings and selected objects show that death carried social and ritual meaning. Archaeology can describe placement, bodies and grave goods; it cannot recover a complete theology. Different burial customs may coexist without representing separate religions or ethnic groups.

Some graves contain rarer ornaments, metalwork or animals, suggesting unequal access and public display. Inequality does not automatically equal a kingdom, hereditary caste or tax state. Researchers need settlements, storage, fortifications, production and repeated mortuary patterns before scaling status into political institutions.

Weapons and defended positions occur in wider plateau records, and trauma can sometimes document violence. This atlas interval offers no evidence for one army controlling the drawn polygon. Raiding, feud, defense and coercion are possible, but naming commanders, enemies or imperial campaigns would be fiction.

Tibetan Buddhism is not an in-period explanation. Museum and textual chronologies place royal patronage, monasteries and Buddhist manuscript culture mainly in the seventh century CE and later, more than a millennium after this card ends. Prehistoric graves should be studied on their own terms rather than called Buddhist.

The Tibetan Empire is also later: its political formation, armies, court records and territorial expansion belong to roughly the seventh through ninth centuries CE. Imperial burial mounds are valuable evidence for that later world, but they cannot supply kings, borders or beliefs for 1500 to 500 BCE.

The outstanding achievement was not a single monument. Communities combined frost-tolerant crops, dairy, varied livestock, mobility, storage, grinding, pottery, textiles and exchange to make lives at altitude. Different solutions fit different valleys and grasslands, which is precisely why one civilization label fits poorly.

Craft was inventive as well as practical: polished ceramics, decorated stone tools, spun fibers and composite metal objects required learned sequences and aesthetic judgment. Similarities reveal communication; differences reveal local choices. Neither pattern needs a plateau-wide ruler issuing designs from one capital.

Modern Tibetic languages form a diverse family derived from Old Tibetan, and many Tibetan-speaking communities have distinct identities. Historical linguistics can model deeper relationships, but this record predates attested Old Tibetan. Archaeological objects inside the polygon cannot tell us exactly which languages their makers spoke.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this atlas category between 1500 and 500 BCE. Tibetan script and the earliest surviving Old Tibetan historical records belong to the imperial era. Supplying Tibetan letters, transliteration and translation here would borrow a voice from more than a thousand years later.

At 500 BCE the exact atlas id disappears; at 400 BCE other broad labels cover many tested places. That editorial switch is not a fall. Farms, herds, routes, households and local traditions continued changing, and much later states and Tibetic literary culture emerged through histories that this polygon cannot summarize.

ending.text: The atlas removes this exact id at 500 BCE. One century later it draws “Proto-Tibetan cultures” across many tested plateau locations and “Zhangzhung kingdom” over several western points, but those are later atlas classifications, not proven successors to one earlier state. The target was never a demonstrated polity, so it did not “fall” as a unit. Local communities, crops, herds, routes and traditions continued and changed. Tibetan script, empire and Buddhist institutions arose much later; none should be used to manufacture a neat ending for this prehistoric umbrella.
